analysis.one_liner: Lets one company own far more broadcast stations, networks, and newspapers by stripping most FCC ownership limits.
analysis.headline: The bill got three days of hearings in May 1995 but never a committee vote, and died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1995, Rep. Cliff Stearns proposed rewriting the Communications Act so the FCC could no longer limit how many broadcast stations, networks, or other media outlets a single company owns. One owner could reach up to 35 percent, then 50 percent, of the national TV audience, and in many cases own two TV stations in the same market. The bill was sent to the House Commerce Committee, got three days of subcommittee hearings, and never received a vote before that Congress ended. The same Congress later passed a broader law, the Telecommunications Act of 1996, that loosened many of the same rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Large broadcast networks and station-group owners. They could buy more stations, reach half the national TV audience, own two stations in one market in many cases, and combine a station with a newspaper or radio outlet. Big-city newspaper publishers also gain the option to buy broadcast stations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big TV networks and station groups

how_it_helps.text: Bars the FCC from issuing or enforcing any rule limiting how many broadcasting stations, networks, or other mass media a single person or company can own, nationally or in any area.

Raises the national TV audience-reach cap: one company could own stations reaching 35 percent of U.S. TV households immediately, and 50 percent after one year, and requires a study of eliminating the cap entirely.
Lets one company own two TV stations in the same market whenever one is a UHF station, and lets the FCC waive the ban for two VHF stations, allowing local 'duopolies'.

analysis.who_pays: Viewers and local communities, who would face fewer independently owned local news voices as stations are bought up by large chains; and smaller independent station owners, who lose bargaining power and come under pressure to sell to bigger groups.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local news viewers and small station owners

drawbacks.text: The bill would concentrate local news ownership: allowing duopolies and up to 50 percent national reach means fewer separate owners deciding what local news gets covered, a cost the bill acknowledges by requiring an FCC study of whether the reach cap should survive.

Supporters' best argument is that the ownership caps dated from the 1940s, before cable and satellite competition, and that financially stronger stations can produce better local programming; the bill's own structure concedes this is a tradeoff, since it still keeps a national cap and same-market limits rather than full deregulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to large broadcast companies, in the form of bigger audiences and market share. The public cost is reduced diversity in local news ownership, which the FCC would only study after the fact, not prevent. Even the bill's defenders describe it as a bet that scale and competition from cable would offset consolidation, and the bill offers no safeguard for local news if that bet fails.

outcome.mechanism: It got three days of hearings in the House telecommunications subcommittee in May 1995, but the full Commerce Committee never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cliff Stearns introduced the bill on May 3, 1995, with nine original cosponsors including Commerce Chairman Thomas Bliley, and it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce.
Five days after introduction it was sent to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, which held hearings on May 10, 11, and 12, 1995.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never reached a subcommittee vote, a full committee markup, or the House floor, and expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large broadcasters lost nothing in the end: this particular bill died, but the same Congress enacted the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which raised the national TV ownership cap to 35 percent and loosened other ownership rules, achieving much of what this bill sought (widely reported). Viewers got no added protection either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large broadcasters, via the 1996 telecom law

for.name: Cliff Stearns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip most FCC broadcast ownership limits and secured nine original cosponsors.

for.name: Thomas Bliley
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original cosponsor; his committee held jurisdiction over it.

for.name: 11 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill within days of its introduction.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote; after three days of subcommittee hearings the bill sat with no action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Ten of the bill's eleven cosponsors were Republicans and one was a Democrat, and no vote was ever taken on the bill itself.

industries.industry: Television networks and large station-group owners
industries.note: The bill lets a single company own stations reaching up to half the national TV audience and two stations in the same market in many cases, shrinking the number of independent owners who decide what local news covers. The company's gain is directly the public's loss of competing local voices.

industries.industry: Newspaper publishers and radio broadcasters (cross-media ownership)
industries.note: The bill bars the FCC from limiting ownership of a broadcast station combined with any other mass medium, opening the door to newspaper-TV and radio-TV combos in the same market. That consolidation concentrates local news into fewer hands.

industries.industry: Small, independent, and minority-owned local stations
industries.note: With consolidation allowed, independent owners face pressure to sell to large groups and lose bargaining power against bigger combined competitors. These owners' interest runs with viewers who want diverse local voices.
